utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-84-T, the Prosecutor versus Ramush Haradinaj et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Re, the Chamber expected to hear the testimony of Witness 30 this afternoon. Could you please update the Chamber and, of course, the public as well on what has happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I have been advised by the Canadian authorities that Witness 30 has been hospitalised since last week when the Canadian authorities were bringing him to the videolink location. He is being examined by a medical practitioner, and the last information we had was on Friday, I think it was, last Friday, which the Canadian authorities said that his position would be reassessed within seven to ten days of that date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The result being that we cannot hear the witness -- the evidence of Witness 30 on this day, which was together with tomorrow, the last days for the presentation of the Prosecution's case. Under those circumstances, the Chamber would like to deal with a few procedural matters, the first one being to deliver a decision on the Prosecution's motion to tender tape and transcript of Ramush Haradinaj addressing a meeting in July 1998. This motion of which I just read the title, was filed on the 19th of November, 2007. The tape and transcript appear to only cover part of the meeting at which Ramush Haradinaj allegedly was present. According to the motion, the tape is part of a larger set of audio recordings provided to the Prosecution by Witness 17. The recording was, however, not tendered through Witness 17 and the only reference to the recording in his testimony is a general reference to tape recordings made of meetings between KLA and FARK representatives. The Defence responded on the 22nd of November, 2007, requesting that the Chamber reject the motion. The Defence pointed to a number of difficulties in determining the relevance and probative value of the material, in particular since the tape and transcript do not contain information about when and where the meeting was held, who was present, and whether matters other than those described in the transcript were discussed at the meeting. In previous decisions on admission of evidence, the Chamber has pointed out that evidence should be presented in a meaningful way in court with proper contextualisation and explanation by witnesses who are in a position to do so. Otherwise, the Chamber has to determine the material's relevance and probative value on the basis of the material itself. The Chamber finds that the tendered material lacks context, and the Chamber is not satisfied that certain vague references in the transcript demonstrate the probative value claimed by the Prosecution. The Chamber understands that what was discussed during the meeting was the relationship between the KLA and FARK. As such, it is relevant; however, this topic has been dealt with extensively by numerous witnesses, including Witness 17. Under these circumstances, the tape and transcript tendered do not assist the Chamber, and the Prosecution's motion is therefore denied. And this concludes the Chamber's decision on this matter. The next decision the Chamber would like to render is the decision on the Prosecution's motion of 23rd of November, 2007 for a further extension of time to its case in order to attempt to secure the testimony of Shefqet Kabashi. The parties will recall that on the 20th of November, 2007, Shefqet Kabashi appeared by videolink and refused to give evidence in this case. At the end of that hearing, the Chamber informed the Prosecution that it would only entertain an application for a further attempt in gaining Mr. Kabashi's testimony if the Prosecution could show that there had been some dramatic changes. The Prosecution was further warned that the Chamber would not engage in an endless continuing story with regard to this witness. Despite the guidance of the Chamber, the Prosecution went ahead with an application for an extension of its case in order to attempt to secure the testimony of Mr. Kabashi at some unspecified date in the future. The Prosecution bases this request on the mere expectation that further contact with his counsel would allow Mr. Kabashi to gain informed advice as to his legal position, with such advice potentially leading Mr. Kabashi to change his mind about not testifying. Mr. Kabashi first refused to testify on the 5th of June, 2007, after which he was advised by counsel as to what the consequences of such a refusal could be. Mr. Kabashi has since reiterated his decision not to testify, most recently at the 20th of November, 2007 hearing. In the present motion, the Prosecution acknowledges that Mr. Kabashi is still unwilling to testify. There has therefore not been any change of circumstances that would warrant a positive response to the Prosecution's motion. Further, the Prosecution seems not to have heeded the Chamber's instruction given during the 20th of November, 2007 hearing, in which it was informed that aside for the exceptional extension until the 27th of November, 2007 in order to hear the evidence of Witness 30, the Chamber considered the Prosecution's case closed. Moreover, the Prosecution has now exceeded the 125 hours that were allotted to it at the beginning of the case. The Chamber will now address the two alternatives put forward by the Prosecution should the Chamber decide not to grant it a further extension of time. The first alternative is to admit Mr. Kabashi's statements under Rule 92 quater. However, Rule 92 quater applies to witnesses who are unavailable to testify due to death, or who can no longer be traced or are unable to testify by reason of bodily or mental condition. Mr. Kabashi is not unavailable due to any of these reasons but is, rather, unwilling to testify. This request is therefore denied. The second alternative put forward is that the Prosecution be allowed to recall Prosecution investigator Barney Kelly, who was present when Mr. Kabashi gave his statements, so as to give hearsay evidence as to the statements provided by Mr. Kabashi to the Prosecution. The Chamber finds this way of introducing evidence which goes to the acts and conduct of the accused, much of it uncorroborated by other evidence, both inappropriate and prejudicial to the Defence, who has had no opportunity to test the veracity of the statements. For the above reasons, the Chamber therefore denies the Prosecution's motion in its entirety. And this concludes the Chamber's decision on the matter. Then I'd like to inform the parties about outstanding decisions or outstanding reasons for decisions already delivered so as to check whether there's no oversight. Outstanding is a decision on admission of evidence in relation to the Stijovic exhibits. Further, there is an outstanding decision on the admission of exhibits which were introduced through Witness 69. Further, there is an outstanding decision on a smaller portion of a Rule 92 quater decision in relation to Witness 1, and reasons are still to be given to -- in relation to those portions of the Rule 92 quater decision which were already decided. Finally, there is still pending a decision on documents the Prosecution seeks to have added to its Rule 65 ter exhibit list. For the annexes A to F of that motion, reasons are still to be delivered, where the decisions have been delivered already. As far as H through K are concerned, the decision is still pending. Finally, there is a decision pending on a motion for protective -- protective measures in relation to Witness 35, and the Chamber expects that a written decision will be filed today. This just serves as a survey of what is still there on the desk of the Chamber. Now I would like to move to -- Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.text: If I might. I've gone through the survey. There may be a couple of other matters that are still pending.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, there are a couple of other matters pending. I'll move on now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: That -- yes, that's the document on my screen. utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: If it should transpire on checking the particular exhibits against the testimony that there is an objection that ought to have been raised at this stage, might I have an hour after the close of court today to communicate the position to the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, any objection against the request?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

Mr. Emmerson, the Chamber checked on the transcript, but, of course, interpreting a transcript, sometimes it's very explicit, sometimes it's just explicit. Then I'd like to move on to agreed facts by the parties. The Chamber has received a joint filing by the parties dated the 23rd of November, 2007, filed on the 26th of November, 2007, in which -- in an attachment to which statement we find facts agreed upon by the parties. It is also indicated -- yes, first of all, I'd like to just briefly remind the parties to what the procedure here is; that if the parties agree on facts -- on matters of law and fact, that they can be invited to file written submissions but Rule 65 ter (H) explains that the final purpose of this is to have them recorded. Therefore, it's now on the record that the parties have filed the submission on the 26th of November and it's put formally on the record as agreed facts. Now, in the motion in which the agreed facts are presented, there is - I think it was in paragraph 3 - there is an observation about -- that there's still ongoing discussions about additional agreed facts on forensic and military issues. Now, the Chamber would very much like to understand at this stage of the proceedings what we are talking about, because during the presentation of the Prosecutor's case, it's the Prosecution who wants to prove or establish certain facts, and therefore it seems logical that the Prosecution then makes proposals which are or are not finally accepted by the Defence. At the same time, if we are in the presentation of the Defence case, the Defence might want to seek certain facts or matters of law to be established and make proposals to the Prosecution to agree to certain issues, certain matters of law and fact, which then might meet or not meet the agreement of the Prosecution. These additional agreed facts, are these agreed facts which under the logic I just described are facts or matters of law the Prosecution would like to establish at this moment, or are we talking about an ongoing discussion on matters which might be -- might be raised during the Defence case, if there will be a Defence case?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I suspect what's happened was it was a draft which the Prosecution put together several months ago --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- and has been circulating ever since and no one ever took the last paragraph out, saying there were ongoing discussions. And it may well be, as Your Honour says, that the Defence may wish to propose some agreed facts. I think we've pretty much exhausted agreed facts in the Prosecution case, unless the Defence has something they can add to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: There is in fact simply one matter, and it doesn't fall directly within the rubric either of scientific facts or military facts. The Trial Chamber may recall that during the testimony of Mijat Stojanovic, he marked two exhibits, which are D27 and D28, which were aerial photographs to the same scale showing the position where he was standing. At the time he claimed to see a man he purported to recognize as my client, and the position where the man was standing. And the one matter which I hope we would be able to reach a formal agreement on is measured electronically through the two photographs, what the distance between those two points is, for the assistance of the Trial Chamber. Both documents are in evidence already. It's a matter of formality --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's just conclusions to be drawn from that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Simply a mechanical measurement of the distance as regards those two. But that's a matter I can deal with with Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Other than --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- that's clear. Then at least the Chamber is aware. Because we would be a bit concerned if there was still an ongoing process.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Other than that, nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because we are talking at this moment whether it was in the -- where there's a small - how do you say it? - where the road bows a bit from to the right of the photograph, rather than from down a bit to the right there.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I don't think that's likely to be contentious. Other than that, I can confirm the correctness of what Mr. Re has indicated. There are no active or ongoing discussions between the parties as far as forensic or military agreed facts are concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that information, Mr. Emmerson. Then I would like to move to a totally different subject matter, which is scheduling. First of all, the Chamber would like to hear from the Defence whether today or, if not, when the Defence could inform the Chamber as to whether there will be a -- any 98 bis application.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think in the past I've indicated that I would request from the Trial Chamber the continuing indulgence that that be an announcement formally made following the formal closure of the Prosecution's case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And so that obviously is the first issue that needs to be resolved. For complete accuracy, I would prefer to make the announcement following receipt of the decisions on the Stijovic and Witness 69 exhibits and the 92 quater application concerning --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- Witness 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: But imminently is the short answer. As soon as those -- as soon as those two matters are, or those two groups of matters are resolved, I'm in a position to indicate on behalf of Mr. Haradinaj what course the Defence proposes to take.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I am similarly situated. As soon as we reach decisions on those matters and we are aware of the Prosecution case being formally closed, we'll be able to formally indicate to the Chamber what we're doing with regard to the 98 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: The Defence has, of course, discussed these matters together, anticipating this question, and my answer is not surprisingly identical to that of my colleagues, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that. One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm seeking one clarification. You have mentioned some decisions. Not all of the decisions I referred to earlier, especially not the decision on the documents on the Rule 65 ter list, that is excluded from your consideration?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: That was an intentional omission, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was intentional. Now, there's one other matter. I said before that the Chamber would deliver this afternoon a written decision on protective measures for Witness 35. Now, there is a possibility that if that decision would deny protective measures, sometimes the Chamber gives a couple of days to the Prosecution to consider whether they want to withdraw or not withdraw that evidence. Would that be time you'd consider to be -- to postpone the close of the Prosecution's case?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No, it won't affect the timetable for the announcement of the decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harvey, the same I see. Then the Chamber expects to deliver these decisions very soon, and therefore we could continue to consider scheduling on the basis - let's just take it as that - that by Wednesday noon the Prosecution's case would be closed. There are then two scenarios: Either we hear from the Prosecution that their -- let me just have a look. The next question would be, if there's no 98 bis, whether the Defence would present a Defence case, because the one is not one decision whether or not to file a 98 bis application is not an indication yet as to whether there will be a Defence case. Now, just for purposes of if there would be no 98 bis decision, then if there would be a Defence case, the Chamber has considered how to proceed. The Chamber would, under those circumstances - and that's a tentative scheduling at this moment which the Chamber puts to the parties for comments - the Chamber would, if there would be a Defence case, expect on the 10th of December to receive the information mentioned in Rule 65 ter (G), that is, witness list with all the information as put in 65 ter (G)(i) and exhibit list as we find it under Rule 65 ter (G)(ii). So that would then be the first date. The second date in the tentative scheduling would be the 12th of December, two days later, a Pre-Defence Conference, and then on the 8th of January, the start of the presentation of evidence on behalf of the Defence. If there would be no Defence case, the Chamber would expect the parties to file final briefs on the 14th of December and is inclined to schedule closing arguments on the 9th and the 10th of January, 2008. The Chamber could not schedule yet what would be the case if there will be a 98 bis application, because the Chamber has some difficulties in assessing how much time it would need the Chamber to give a decision on that. So if that would be the case, then, of course, other scheduling proposals will reach the parties. I'd like to give an opportunity to the parties - perhaps you first, Mr. Re - to the tentative scheduling as I just mentioned it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: If there is -- if the Defence -- if you get to the stage where there's a -- either no 98 bis decision -- sorry, no 98 bis application or the 98 bis application or decision after the application is against the Defence, the Prosecution would very much ask the Trial Chamber to direct the Defence to inform the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution as to whether the accused are -- would be testifying; and if so, in what order. And we would want that information on the date that the -- well, as soon as possible, basically, but definitely on the date that the -- when the Defence has to file their pre-trial list of witnesses -- sorry, their pre-defence list of witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. From what I remember, it's good English tradition that the accused who wants to testify testifies first. That's not a tradition in all jurisdictions. Mr. Emmerson, could you respond to this request and could you also further comment on the observations the -- or the tentative scheduling the Chamber expressed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. Can I take them in reverse order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So far as the tentative schedule outlined by the Trial Chamber in the event of there being no 98 bis submission but a Defence positive case is concerned, I have no observations to make. The timetable is one within which we would be comfortable to work and incorporated within that, if there is a communication to be made to Mr. Re on the 10th of December, that, of course, will include a communication as regards individual accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's as soon as on the 10th of December, you would then provide the Chamber or -- yes, the Chamber with your witness list and the exhibit list. You would then --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: That's what I understood Mr. Re was inviting us to confirm.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It has to be done by that date, clearly. I mean, the accused have to be included in the list of -- of any witnesses. The Prosecution wants that information before that date. I would ask the Trial Chamber to set a schedule which includes notification of -- of those dates so the Prosecution is in a position to be properly prepared, if, for example, the accused were to testify immediately after the resumption of the court, after the recess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, Mr. Emmerson, the Chamber would invite the Defence -- let's just again work on the basis of the assumption that the Chamber has delivered all -- all decisions by Wednesday noon. It could even be earlier. Then the Chamber would invite the Defence to -- to -- of course, we would then immediately hear whether there will be any 98 bis application; if so, we will make further scheduling efforts. If there would be no 98 bis, then the Chamber would like to hear whether there will be a Defence case at all. Preferably not later than two days after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would be the 30th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm optimistic that we -- particularly if we know we have reached a final position so far as the Prosecution's tendering of evidence is concerned, I'm optimistic that we will be in a position to inform the Trial Chamber both as regards 98 bis and as regards, at least in broad terms, the shape of any Defence case, very, very shortly after the Prosecution's case is closed. utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That would mean that the Chamber, at least on the 30th of November, would know --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Certainly by then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- If there would -- certainly by that date. Okay. That's then on the record. You said you would. The Chamber makes it a deadline as well, so that's unless any of the other Defence counsel would have any observations to be made in respect of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No, I'm more than happy to work with those dates. Those dates make sense to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And Mr. Harvey, I see that you're in agreement, just by your body language, nodding "yes."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Nodding again. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And as regards the alternative state of affairs, that is to say, in the event of there being no 98 bis decision and no Defence case called, may we reserve the right at this stage to return to the Trial Chamber with observations as to the appropriate final date for filing closing briefs?

utterances.text: Yes, final briefs then -- what I said, 14th of December. You would like to consider whether that would cause you problems. utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Our preference would be longer for the written than for the oral.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'd like the opportunity to consult with my colleagues on the Haradinaj Defence and, of course, with those representing Mr. Balaj and Mr. Brahimaj and respond to the Trial Chamber's suggestion with, if I can put it this way, a -- an -- a unified alternative proposal. It may be that in the scenario postulated we won't be very far apart from the Prosecution's suggestion, but I -- I am reluctant to respond to that, so to speak, immediately on my feet without having had an opportunity just to consider it with others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll find further ways of communication to -- to discuss these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There's one other matter I would like to raise here as well. If not later than this Friday, the 30th of November, the Chamber and the Prosecution would be informed as to - if there's no 98 bis application - whether there will be a Defence case, would there be any possibility - and I'm not just thinking in terms of what this Chamber needs, but also in view of what this Tribunal needs - would there be any possibility to already receive information, in whatever at this stage vague form, either expressed in numbers of witnesses or --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- numbers or weeks or months, or hours needed to present the evidence --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- in chief, so that, also in view of the consequences it may have for other cases, that we have at least some awareness of what to expect?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Absolutely. And as I -- as I indicated perhaps elliptically a little while ago, if we are in a position that the Prosecution's case is closed, for example, by noon tomorrow, I would expect to be in a position to give the Trial Chamber some very clear information within a very short time thereafter. And by -- by "a short time," I can conceive of it being in a matter of hours, and certainly no longer than a day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that answer, which, Mr. Guy-Smith and Mr. Harvey --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It will not be a problem to give the Chamber information in more than a vague form but less than a definite form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, the definite form we expect at the 65 ter (G) list. Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I will be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Affirmative nodding.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I will be in a similar position, yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you'd just give me one second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. When I earlier gave this summary of outstanding decisions, of course there -- there might be smaller ones, but the Chamber focused on decisions on evidence; although, we've mentioned a few others as well. And may I take it, Mr. Emmerson, the ones I mentioned, and the ones you specifically mentioned where you said, These three decisions we'd like to have received before we give any further information about 98 bis or -- and soon after that, that you limited them to these three decisions? Or are there any others in which --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, I limited it to those three decisions. And, again, I may have expressed myself somewhat elliptically, but I indicated as far as those were concerned, it would be our preference to know the precise position in relation to those three decisions before expressing a view as to 98 bis. Obviously, there may be material upon which the Trial Chamber then has a ruling to make. But the sooner we are in a position of saying that the Prosecution's case is -- is formally closed, the sooner we will be in a position to respond in respect of -- of 98 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is there any further matter to be raised at this moment? Because I'm through my agenda, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Could I just indicate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- there is one very minor matter that I wanted to raise. utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, I think there are two questions: First, whether you are going to disclose the judgement itself; and when.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: We don't have it. So we're not going to disclose it, because we don't have it. If the Defence wishes to get the judgement, they can make the relevant inquiries of the Swiss authorities. utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This document -- you referred to "this document in the Prosecution's possession since 2006," and "this document" did not refer to the judgement.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. Just to remind the Trial Chamber, the position is this: A very short time before Mr. Krasniqi was due to testify, the Prosecution disclosed the documents that had been in their possession for over a year, indicating that there was a judgement and conviction in absentia. And obviously the very late disclosure of that material placed the Defence and all parties in an impossible position properly to explore the credibility issues that this gives rise to with the witness whilst he was testifying. And therefore at page 10775, line 1, I made on the record in front of Mr. Re, I believe, a formal request that the Prosecution complete its disclosure obligations in respect of this document by obtaining the judgement to which it refers and which they, in our submission, most certainly, should have obtained for the purposes of Rule 68 in June of 2006, rather than providing this material to the Defence at the time when it was in practical terms useless for deployment in cross-examination, because it couldn't be explored in relation to the substance. Now, the witness then gave certain answers, and obviously one would want to be in a position to compare those answers with the judgements. If it is not available, in other words, if the Prosecution does not complete its Rule 68 obligations, as we submit they are, then we will be making certain submissions to the Trial Chamber in due course about how it is proper to approach the evaluation of the witness's credibility when the Prosecution has not properly disclosed material which is potentially relevant to his credibility. The fact of the matter is this is all part and parcel of the Prosecution's Rule 68 obligations and they made it impossible for the Defence to obtain the material for deployment in a reasonable time by sitting on these documents - I can't use any other word for it - sitting on these documents for a period of approaching 17 months.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There's no -- Mr. Emmerson well knows --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please. Yes. I would like to hear your submissions on this matter. I formulate it as neutral as possible, because the Chamber is more interested in the results than in a judgement and who is to be blamed for what. Could you assist in any way, Mr. Re?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, if Mr. Emmerson had any authority to the -- legal authority to the effect that the Prosecution has a legal obligation, as he seems to assert, to obtain material, that is, to go trawling through Swiss archives or somewhere to find material for the Defence, he would have referred the Trial Chamber to it. In fact, the case law of the Tribunal is directly against Mr. Emmerson's proposition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's -- let's -- I'm going to interrupt you there. Was there an obligation already once Mr. Krasniqi was on the witness list to disclose this -- this disclosed material which seems to be of an exculpatory nature?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Clearly. And the fact is we disclosed it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So -- yes but --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I know that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. But --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I can't take away from the fact that it was late, but we did disclose it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was late. utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I think I -- I think I might have a -- I might have a solution. Once again, it's in the hands of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: But it seems the quickest way of getting information and the most practicable way of getting information would be for the Prosecution to send a request for assistance to the -- to the Swiss authorities, as they've done previously. And probably the case will be well over before we get it. But I suggest to you that perhaps using the request for assistance mechanisms that they have used repeatedly in other situations may well be the quickest way for us to get the information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: May I just make a practical suggestion?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At the same time, this interrupted Mr. Re's answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.speaker: MR. RE

utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes D223.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Registrar. utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well,--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

An order from the Trial Chamber directed towards the Swiss authorities, may be quicker. It's just a matter of speed. utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now you introduced a new element, which I clearly wanted to exclude. utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

And finally, if they really go to the substance of issues, that they then should be filed, but then the Chamber will give instructions. utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any further matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There are two -- two other matters I'd like to deal with. One is a correction to the record, something I said earlier on a different day. And there is another one. utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll consider that in a second, Mr. Re. The second issue you'd like to raise was?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I said it's a correction to the record. On the 22nd of October, I was referring -- in relation to Branko Gajic and questions about the Prosecution -- what the Prosecution had put to Bozidar Delic in the Milosevic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there a page and a line?

utterances.text: Yes. I'm just about to tell you. It's at page 9656. I said: "There was no specific allegation of criminality leveled against Delic, as far as I can see." utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There are four summaries. I think about five minutes each.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Five minutes each. I think then it would be better to have a break first, so in order not to -- unless I get a clear message from joint teams that they would prefer to continue and then to be off the hook for the remainder of the day. But, Mr. Guy-Smith, you --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. With regard to the correction made by Mr. Re. There seemed to be two component parts to that. One was his review of the Milosevic transcript and the other was talking to lawyers who were in court conducting the cross-examination. I'm not sure whether or not he's correcting both of those matters or just one of them. And would -- would appreciate some clarification in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The representation was made not only with regard to the transcript itself but also with regard to conversations that he had had with people who were responsible --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- for conducting cross-examination in regards to the criminality --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you reviewed or have you re-thought your recollection on such discussions, or was it just on the basis of your review now of the transcript that you came to the conclusion that what you said, and for which you gave two sources, whether that was not correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No, I based -- no, no, I -- no, I don't correct the second part. I based part of what I said in talking to lawyers who were in court conducting their cross-examination. There is a lawyer here, a senior trial attorney, who I specifically --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- spoke to before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- speaking to the Trial Chamber. There's nothing to correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Reviewing your conclusion, was based exclusively on your review of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Absolutely. Completely on review of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So let's not try to get into further detail on who might then have not given correct information. I'm looking at the booth now.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We would prefer a break, if for nothing else than at least to get the documents from -- from the Prosecution that they will be reading from. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is a perfect reason to have a break. We will have a break and we'll resume at ten minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Two matters before we start hearing the 92 ter summaries. Mr. Re [sic], I promised you one hour after we would have adjourned for P1229. If you by any chance would have made up your mind already, it saves you sending an e-mail; or perhaps not.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The answer is, yes, there is no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then P1229 is admitted now, finally, into evidence. Mr. Re, when you read the 92 ter statements, could you please spend half an ear on the French translation or invite someone else to do that so that everyone can hear what you read. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'll share -- I'll share the reading duties with Mr. Di Fazio. The first one is the summary of Witness 64, who testified on the 3rd of September, 2007, at pages 7818 to pages 7888 of the transcript. The Witness summary of Witness 64 is the following: Witness 64 has been a police officer since 1992. His first assignment was with the SUP in Pec, or Peja. He was stationed there until 14th of June, 1999, when the MUP and VJ had to leave Kosovo after the NATO bombing. He works with the Service for Combatting Organised Crime, as part of the Crime Police Department of the Serbian MUP. His specialty is crime scene technician. The witness says that the Dukagjin Zone in Kosovo is also known as "Metohija" in Serbian. He -- his statement gives evidence about a number of apparent KLA attacks on Serbs in the Dukagjin Zone in 1998. The witness first arrived at the Lake Radonjic Canal on the 11th of September, 1998. His function was to video record the scene. When he first approached the canal, the witness saw about five or six bodies by the wall of the canal. Further down from the first five or six bodies, he saw two bodies near where the water falls about 5 metres to the canyon. These bodies were covered with stones and earth. On the 11th of September, 1998, the witness began to record by video the scene at Lake Radonjic to get an overview before the forensic experts began numbering the bodies. The witness also followed the forensics experts and video-recorded their work. Bodies were marked with labels such as "R-1", and so on. The "R" stood for Radonjic, and the numbers identified each body sequentially. When each body was examined by the forensic experts, it was put into a body-bag with its identifying number. Later the bodies were put into a truck. None of the victims were wearing uniforms and all were dressed in civilian clothing. The witness could see bullet holes through the victims' clothing. Some bodies were tied with barbed wire on their bodies. One body had a rope around its neck. The witness made video recordings of the canal at Lake Radonjic, the Ekonomija farm (which also had a hazelnut farm), Glodjane village, Hotel Pastrik, and other scenes between 11th of September and 26th of September, 1998. The recordings were made on three videotapes which were provided to the Office of the Prosecutor at the ICTY. That completes the summary for Witness 64. Mr. Di Fazio has one for Mr. Kelly. MR. DI FAZIO: Two in fact, if Your Honours please. The summary of the 92 ter statement of Barney Kelly relating to exhumations. Mr. Barney Kelly is an investigator working for the Office of the Prosecutor. He was a police officer in the Irish police. Since 2004, he has been involved in the investigation of this case involving these three accused. His primary focus has been on the areas around Lake Radonjic, the Ekonomija farm, and Dasinovac. Mr. Kelly describes how the Serbian authorities discovered a number of bodies in these areas in September 1998. He describes how post-mortem examinations were conducted at the Hotel Pastrik in Djakovica. Mr. Kelly explains that a number of bodies were identified by relatives using traditional means. This involves the identification of human remains by clothing, personal property located on or near the remains, old injuries, and so on. Four of the victims were identified as Vukosava Markovic, Darinka Kovac, Isuf Hoxha, and Hajrullah Gashi. In 2005, in order to carry out DNA testing of these human remains amongst others, Mr. Kelly contacted relatives of the victims, including those already mentioned, with a view to obtaining their consent for the exhumation of the remains in order to carry out DNA testing. He also sought blood samples from the relatives to permit DNA testing to be carried out. In early August 2005, Mr. Kelly travelled to Piskote cemetery, where the human remains of Vukosava Markovic and Darinka Kovac were thought to be, but found the cemetery to be overgrown with vegetation and realized that he would need assistance of relatives to locate the bodies. In mid-August 2005, Mr. Kelly approached the family of Hajrullah Gashi, seeking permission to exhume his remains; however, the family withheld its consent. In late August 2005, Mr. Kelly went to Piskote cemetery and relatives of Vukosava Markovic and Darinka Kovac pointed out the supposed burial site of those two women. On the 7th of October, 2005, Mr. Kelly went to Piskote cemetery and two grave sites were excavated. One grave site -- one grave yielded the remains of woman, but the other grave had the remains of two adults, a baby, and a child. The remains of the woman were collected and handed to OMPF representatives. The grave, which had revealed the two adults, baby, and child, were filled in again. On the 11th of October, 2005, the remains from the first grave were forensically examined and ascertained to be those of a woman aged 60 years or more and DNA samples were extracted from the bones. Subsequent DNA analysis revealed that the remains could not be those of Darinka Kovac or Vukosava Markovic. On the 21st of October, 2005, Mr. Kelly again sought permission from the family of Hajrullah Gashi permitting exhumation of his remains, but permission was again refused. On the 22nd of October, Mr. Kelly attempted to locate the grave of Hajrullah Gashi himself at Prizren Muslim cemetery, but with no success. In late November 2005, Mr. Kelly travelled to Podgorica Police Station and obtained the consent of a relative of Isuf Hoxha to exhume his remains and obtained a blood sample from this relative with a view to obtaining DNA identification of any remains that might be found. Mr. Kelly had reservations about the remains disinterred in October 2005 being those of Darinka Kovac or Vukosava Markovic, and therefore in late November 2005 he contacted relatives again with a view to revisiting the Piskote cemetery. He obtained a blood sample from a relative of both women. He spoke to other relatives of both women and obtained information of a possible alternative grave site within the same cemetery. On the 5th of December, 2005, Mr. Kelly travelled to Djakovica Muslim cemetery with a relative of Isuf Hoxha, but the location of the grave of Isuf Hoxha could not be located. On the 9th of December, 2005, Mr. Kelly went to Piskote cemetery again with relatives of Darinka Kovac and Vukosava Markovic. The cemetery was again looked at with a view to locating the grave sites and an area was pointed out by relatives as the area where the two women were buried in 1998. On the 12th of December, 2005, the area was exhumed but no remains were found. On the 10th of December, 2005, Mr. Kelly again sought permission from the family of Hajrullah Gashi to exhume his remains, but again permission was refused. That completes that summary. I'll read the -- a second summary of the 92 ter statement of Barney Kelly relating to photo-boards. He testified on the 25th of June, and his testimony is to be found at trial transcript references 6070 to 6115. Mr. Barney Kelly is an investigator working for the Office of the Prosecutor. He was a police officer in the Irish Police. Since 2004, he has been involved in investigation of this case involving the three accused. Mr. Kelly interviewed Witness 17 on the 10th and 11th of November, 2004, and again from the 21st to the 26th of November, 2004. During the course of the interviews, Mr. Kelly produced 19 photo-boards to the witness. The photo-boards were in colour, and each had eight photographs of individuals on them, with each photograph numbered from 1 to 8. Mr. Kelly asked the witness to write down the name and corresponding number of the photograph of any person he recognized on a piece of yellow adhesive paper and stick it underneath the photo. The witness proceeded to do that in the presence of Mr. Kelly and the interpreter present. The witness marked two photographs from two photo-boards as depicting the accused Ramush Haradinaj. Both the photo-boards are annexed at Annex A to Mr. Kelly's statement. The witness marked three photographs from three photo-boards as depicting the accused Lahi Brahimaj. The three photo-boards are annexed as Annex B to Mr. Kelly's statement. The witness marked one photograph from one photo-board as depicting the accused Idriz Balaj. This photo-board is annexed as Annex C to Mr. Kelly's statement. The witness marked three photographs from three photo-boards as depicting Nazmi Brahimaj. The three photo-boards are annexed as Annex D to Mr. Kelly's statement. The witness marked three photographs from three photo-boards as depicting Alush Agushi. The three photo-boards are annexed as Annex E to Mr. Kelly's statement. The witness marked two photographs from two photo-boards as depicting Fadil Nimani, also known as Tigri. The two photo-boards are annexed as Annex F to Mr. Kelly's statement. The witness did not recognize anyone from some of the photo-boards. Those photo-boards are annexed as Annex G. Although Mr. Kelly took a statement from the witness in which these identification procedures are discussed, he overlooked including any reference to the witness identifying Alush Agushi.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The next one is the summary, the 92 ter summary statement of Zarko Bajectic, who testified on the 27th of June, 2007, at pages 6358 to 6458 and his statement is Exhibit P377. From July through October/November 1998, the witness was posted to the State Security - that's the RDB - in Djakovica. The witness was sent to Djakovica to investigate the criminal/terrorist activities and organisational structure of the KLA. The RDB Djakovica was responsible for the Dukagjini Zone. The RDB investigated kidnappings and murders carried out by the KLA. The witness described in his statement how the RDB collected information on the organisational structure of the KLA and on its members. The Dukagjini Zone came under absolute KLA control from March 1998 onwards. The witness states that the KLA Dukagjini Zone was under the command of Ramush Haradinaj from the village of Glodjane. Toger, or Idriz Balaj, was in charge of the Black Eagles. This unit, the Black Eagles, was used to kidnap people and commit murders. They wore black uniforms. Lahi Brahimaj was in charge of the unit in Jablanica. He was Ramush Haradinaj's uncle. The smuggling of weapons by the KLA from Albania was organised by Ramush Haradinaj. This began in March 1998 after the conflict at Prekaz. Weapons were smuggled across the Albanian border either on foot or on horses to Smonica village. From March 1998 onwards, the fighting between the KLA and MUP continued and intensified. The Dukagjini area had become inaccessible from March 1998. The villages were inaccessible unless an operation was staged by the MUP. Such an operation was staged by the MUP in September 1998 after the MUP and RDB received information of bodies located in the Lake Radonjic Canal area. An operation was launched to investigate and recover bodies in that area. On the 10th of September, 1998, the witness attended the Lake Radonjic Canal area and saw bodies. He later attended the Dasinovac crime site as well. The next one is the Rule 92 summary -- 92 ter summary of Witness 28, who testified on the 1st of November, 5th of November, and 6th of November at pages 10162 to 10301 of the transcript. And this is one which I started to read on the 1st of November and we paused to review it. In 1998, the witness worked as a human rights worker for the Humanitarian Law Centre, a Belgrade-based NGO, and travelled frequently to Kosovo to investigate crimes committed by both Albanians and Serbs. A Serb researcher investigated crimes committed against Serbs, and Albanian researchers interviewed -- researched crimes committed against Albanians. They travelled to areas of conflict to investigate whether crimes had been committed. In 1998, the witness was in Kosovo for about a week to ten days every month, with other researchers investigated crimes committed in the Dukagjini area. In early March 1998, the witness went to Cirez/Likoshani following a MUP attack. Survivors reported the police attacking armed [sic] civilians in their homes. The police had blamed the villagers for hiding "terrorists." Following the attack on the Jashari family compound in Prekaz on about the 5th of March, 1999 -- 1998, I'm sorry, the witness travelled there to investigate and witnessed Albanians digging up bodies in a field, preparing to rebury them. The witness investigated the attack and found out that Adem Jashari was known within some Serbian police circles as the "Albanian Arkan" and was known as a local criminal with a close relationship to the local police chief. HLC researchers interviewed witnesses to the attack on the Haradinaj family compound of 24th of March, 1998. That was the last time that HLC researchers were allowed access to KLA-controlled areas in the Decani municipality. An HLC researcher was stopped at a check-point in April 1998 at Pozar on the way to Glodjane and refused access by Daut Haradinaj. From then onwards, MUP patrols and officers were regularly attacked on the main road. In April 1998, Serb and Montenegrin refugees in Babaloc told the witness that the KLA had been using grenade launchers and shooting every day and night at the settlement and that it had been under attack since late 1997. Three witnesses -- sorry, three houses in it had been blown up by the KLA by the end of April 1998. Then the last week of April 1998, the witness counted 34 Serb families that had left their villages in the Dukagjini area. The witness calculated that 123 Serb families had been living in Decan in early 1998. HLC researchers established that by the 19th of April, 1998, some Serbs had been ordered by the KLA to leave their villages and some had left in fear, having previously been the target of attacks. By the 21st of April, 1998, the last Serb families had left their villages. Milovan and Milka Vlahovic's daughter told the witness that on the 20th, the 21st of April, armed KLA came to Gornji Ratis and were shooting in the air at Serb houses. As a result, the Serbs left their houses. By the 12th of April, the only Serbs remaining in Dasinovac were Slobodan Radosevic, Milos Radunovic, and the Markovic family. The witness interviewed Stanisa Radosevic, who had been taken to Glodjane KLA HQ and badly beaten. The witness observed an escalation of the conflict between the KLA and police and KLA and VJ along the border from March 1998 onwards. Almost no civilian traffic was on the Pristina-Djakovica-Decani road by the end of April. Bus services were no longer operating on the Pristina-Djakovica-Pec road from the end of April. And I'm using the Serbian names, it being a Serbian witness. By the end of May, the police could not keep that road open and the witness had to detour by roads north of Pec. On 24th or 25th of May, 1998, while in Pec, the witness heard of two police being kidnapped by the KLA near Prilep. The witness travelled to Dolovo to investigate reports of conflict and heard shooting and found the MUP in the village and houses on fire and animals dead on the road. By the end of April, it was clear that the KLA was expanding its territory and mobilising villagers. Much information pointed to Ramush Haradinaj as a KLA commander in Dukagjini. In mid-1998, the KLA [sic] had information on the KLA structure in Glodjane, naming the three main officials as Shkelzen, Daut, and Ramush Haradinaj. KLA attacks on MUP patrols provoked retaliation by the MUP, which indiscriminately shelled and burned Albanian houses and killed Albanian civilians. Albanian males then joined the KLA. The witness contributed to the HLC's Spotlight Reports published in 1998.

utterances.text: This is the Rule 92 ter summary of Major-General Branko Gajic. Branko Gajic retired as a major-general in the VJ and deputy head of the security administration, the UB, in 2001. Military intelligence had an independent unit in Kosovo, the 14th Counter-Intelligence Group in Pristina, which reported directly to the UB in Belgrade. The witness made about 15 to 20 --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In January 1998, the witness met all counter-intelligence officers who were part of the 3rd Army. Mr. Gajic became aware of the KLA in the mid-1990s after reading its communiques which claimed responsibility for period killings and attacks. I'm about, I think, eight lines in, for the interpreters in the booths. I did not hear any French. Was that -- was that me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you say, "I did not hear any French. Was that me?" That is a bit of a puzzle to me. I will listen to the French channel. If you'd please continue, Mr. Re. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When he visited Kosovo in late 1997, he was unable to enter areas near Djakovica and Pec. In 1997, there were 55 attacks against VJ along the border and 51 attacks in the rest of Kosovo. This increased dramatically in 1998. He received reports of -- he received reports of KLA activities, including the organisation of village staffs, imposition of curfews, threats and beatings of Albanians opposed to the KLA. He received reports that the Babaloc Serb refugee settlement was shelled at the end of February 1998. The witness read many reports of Serbian homes being attacked by the KLA (such as those in Bec on the 2nd of March, 1998). KLA activity intensified after the attack on the Jashari compound on the 5th of March, 1998. It increased its attacks on police patrols and increased weapons smuggling across the Albanian border. Military convoys travelled in heavily armed convoys. Mr. Gajic received what he considered as reliable estimates of 3.000 armed KLA fighters, with 3.000 additional unarmed, by the 17th of April, 1998. Colonel Bozidar Delic of the 549th Motorised Brigade requested a state of emergency from the FRY government on the 5th of March, 1998. Gajic was then receiving daily reports of KLA weapons smuggling. The 52nd Military Police Battalion deployed at the southern end of Lake Radonjic in March 1998 was to "act as a bone in the throat" of the KLA. Delic ordered combat readiness on the 22nd of April, 1998 and assessed the strength of the KLA there at 500 "armed terrorists." The VJ was preoccupied with ensuring border post security after March 1998 and Kosare was the most frequently attacked post. In April 1998, the 549th Brigade reported that nearly all able-bodied men were armed and that an effort was underway to forcibly arm Catholic Albanians. General Gajic received reports of hundreds of KLA members crossing the border in May 1998. On the 7th of May, the FRY government widened the border zone to 5 kilometres in the area in which the VJ was authorised to conduct operations. The witness received reports in May 1998 of the VJ discovering large quantities of weaponry at the border and of KLA military organisation. In over ten armed clashes, 23 KLA members were killed, six were captured, and many were wounded. A report dated the 11th of May, 1998, accurately, in the witness's opinion, says that "all the villages" on the north of the Junik-Djakovica road were fully armed. On the 13th of May, General Pavkovic estimated that the KLA held 30 per cent of Kosovo and had between 3 and a half thousand and 4 and a half thousand men. The KLA attempted to link areas under its control in Dukagjini with Drenica. General Lazarevic warned of this on a report of the 13th of May, 1998. The KLA frequently attacked MUP and KLA convoys along the roads. A Pristina Corps report of 17th of May, 1998 shows that the KLA was successful and General Lazarevic suspended convoys along the Pristina-Klina-Djakovica road and others. On the 20th of May, 1998, the Pristina Corps forward command post estimated that 30 per cent of Kosovo was under KLA control, with 10.000 armed individuals, including 5.000 actually participating in the activities. In a particularly intense attack against a MUP convoy on the 24th of May, 1998, the KLA fired rocket-propelled grenades and automatic weapons from both sides of the road at Prilep. On the 25th of May, the MUP launched a counteroffensive after the abduction of police officers Rade Popadic and Nikola Jovanovic. A VJ report on the 26th of May refers to the KLA as mobilising against the MUP counteroffensive at Prilep. That completes that summary. And for the record, Branko Gajic testified on the 22nd and 23rd of October, 2007, at pages 9665 to 9813 of the transcript.
